newsitem.title: USA: Mass Lt. Gov sees budget approved by deadline.
newsitem.headline: Mass Lt. Gov sees budget approved by deadline.

text.p: Massachusetts Lt. Gov. Paul Cellucci has predicted that the state likely would reach a new budget by the July 1 deadline although the House and Senate each have approved their own different pacts.

"I hope we have one by July 1 but that's not certain. I think we'll probably make it," Cellucci told Reuters on Wednesday at the Annual Conference of the New England Governors and Eastern Canadian Premiers.

Cellucci was unfazed by the possibility that the state might miss the deadline for the start of the 1998 fiscal year, as well as by comments made by U.S. Senator Jesse Helms, R-N.C., who said he planned to oppose the nomination of Massachusetts Gov William Weld as ambassador to Mexico.
Should Helms prevail, that could complicate next year's gubernatorial race, as Cellucci is considered a potential front-runner and would benefit from be named acting governor without long delays.

Saying Helms had made similar remarks in the past, Cellucci said he thought Weld could make a compelling case for winning the ambassadorship, citing the Gov's experience as a U.S. associate attorney general.

"When Bill Weld does go to Mexico City, I'm going to focus on doing my job, getting some things done for the people of Massachusetts, and I'm going to try to put the political stuff second," he said. "And I know there's an election next year, but if I do a good job I think that's going to give me credibility to present my case to the voters next fall."

Noting that in the past four or five years Massachusetts has done a much better job of getting its budgets approved on time, Cellucci said that if failed to do so this time around, the state likely would adopt a one-month contingency budget for one month, in which case the state government would be funded at 1/12th of the 1997 fiscal pact. Or perhaps a shorter, one-week pact would be put in place, for 1/52nd of the present rate of spending.

Among the disputes still unresolved is a difference over whether the state should use about $134 million of a projected surplus to make the last payment on bonds issued in the late 1980s to help the state pay for operating expenses during its fiscal crisis, a step supported only by the Senate, as well as how to divy up the rest of the estimated $400 million surplus.
Cellucci has said the Weld Administration wants to use the windfall, the result of an improving economy, to pay for tax cuts, additional debt repayment and possibly, one-time capital projects.

Another major issue that has yet to be worked out is how Massachusetts will spend an approximately $100 million windfall from the federal grant for welfare that Boston is expected to get for each of the next four or five years.

Massachusetts was one of the first states to adopt new programs that shift welfare recipients to workfare, and because it has cut rolls, it will get extra money from Washington, which is basing the grants under its new law, which has a similar emphasis, on the previous number of people collecting benefits.

"We want some of that money set aside in case there's a downturn in the economy, we want to put some of that money into daycare and the kinds of things that will make welfare reform work," Cellucci said. He added no specific amounts for these programs had been earmarked.

Tax cuts proposed by the Weld Administration so far have faced a bit of an uphill battle in the legislature, but Cellucci said even if they were not included in the budget, it was prepared to resubmit them as a separate package.

One tax reduction that appeared likely to win approval in some form was a proposal to help families by raising a deduction against income taxes to $1,600 from $600--although this is the biggest dollar amount that has been proposed.
While the Senate wants to raise the deduction to $1,000, the House would be a bit more generous, suggesting $1,200.
"But it looks like we're going to get something because even though there are three bills, they're all moving in the same direction," the Lt Gov said.

He was less optimistic about a plan to abolish county governments in the state, noting that only Senate had include the proposal in its budget. Asked about the odds of getting the measure approved, he answered: "I'd say about fifty-fifty."

Still, that assessment was more positive than the one he offered for another measure, which would shift probation from the courts to the public safety department. "That doesn't seem to be going anywhere in the legislature."
